title: When to Cut Price for Strategy, Not for Sales
documentTitle: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech) — PTX0417: Email from Jonathan Bellack to Eisar Lipkovitz et al. (November 10, 2016)
excerptForBlog:
I can be there. However in the Jedi++ meeting you are going to see data that lowering the sell-side revshare does not look like it is going to have tactical benefit. It doesn't win many queries compared to the profit lost, and sales does not think it will help them win deals. So if we still wanted to do it it would need to be for strategic reasons, belief that it would be better for our longer-term market position.

I went this route before, if we lower margin on the sell side we just need to acknowledge we can't recoup on DBM/AdX Buyers. I never claimed that this is a direct play of giving up margin to gain volume. This is more of competitive market situation with strategic play. As I thought about this more my desire to lower margin shrunk, but I still think a token reduction coupled with transparency and the launch of Exchange Bidding is a powerful combo. We should use the time to brainstorm and explain to Sridhar our current thinking and not just focus on margins.

lessonTitle: When to Cut Price for Strategy, Not for Sales
pullQuote: A price cut with no strategic story is just margin you gave away for nothing.
leadershipTraits: Honest about being wrong — walks back his own earlier proposal without defensiveness
Separates data from strategy — knows when numbers rule out a tactic but don't rule out a bet
Focuses the agenda — redirects the team from one metric to the whole strategic question
Thinks in bundles — combines price, transparency, and product into a single market signal
situation: In November 2016, Google ad product executive Jonathan Bellack wrote to a group of colleagues about a planned meeting on 'Jedi++,' an internal ad-tech pricing initiative. The core question: should Google lower the revenue share it takes on the sell side of its ad exchange? Data from the meeting would show the cut wouldn't win many extra auctions, and the sales team didn't think it would help close deals either.
insight: Bellack is doing something disciplined here: he's separating tactical logic from strategic logic. He writes plainly that lowering the sell-side margin 'doesn't look like it is going to have tactical benefit' — it won't move the needle on volume. But he doesn't stop there. He argues the move could still be worth doing for 'strategic reasons' and 'longer-term market position.' That's a different kind of argument entirely. He also names the constraint clearly: if you cut margin on the sell side, 'we just need to acknowledge we can't recoup on DBM/AdX Buyers.' No pretending the money comes back another way. His final position is telling — his enthusiasm for the cut 'shrunk,' but he still sees value in a small, symbolic reduction paired with transparency and the launch of Exchange Bidding. That's a bundled signal to the market: we're open, we're competing fairly, here's proof. The framework is competitive positioning, not margin optimization.
application: Before you cut your price, ask which problem you're actually solving. If the data says it won't win deals, stop calling it a sales move — own it as a market-positioning move, define what 'winning' looks like in that frame, and make sure your team agrees on the constraint it creates elsewhere in your economics.
